issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of trauma to a loved one. 'Being looked at sexually' implies a sexual-threat/self-directed trauma context that is not supported anywhere else in the profile and is hard to reconcile with bereavement/trauma-to-loved-one as the index trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: Within the Triggers node, the items do not form a coherent theme. 'Talking about the future' could fit grief-related loss, but 'incomprehensible chatter' and especially 'being looked at sexually' point toward very different trauma contexts, making the trigger profile internally inconsistent for a single index trauma.

vignette:
Samuel is a 63-year-old journalist, married, and originally from West Africa. He came to therapy at his wife’s urging, though he admits he has been struggling for months. The event that haunts him is not his own injury but the slow, incomprehensible death of his younger brother, Kwame, in a hospital in Accra two years ago. Samuel had flown home when Kwame’s condition worsened after a routine surgery turned septic. For three days, Samuel sat by the bed, listening to the doctors and nurses speak rapidly in Twi and English, their words blurring into a frantic, incomprehensible chatter that he could not parse. He held Kwame’s hand as his brother’s breathing became shallow, and in the final hour, a metallic, coppery taste filled Samuel’s own mouth—a taste that returns to him now, unbidden, whenever a memory surfaces. What devastates Samuel most is that he cannot tell the story properly. When his wife asks what happened, or when a colleague offers condolences, Samuel opens his mouth, but the thread vanishes. He knows exactly what he saw and felt, but the words scatter like startled birds. He loses the thread, trails off, and is left standing there, mute, as if the event itself has stolen his language.

The triggers are everywhere, and each one pulls him back into that hospital room. Talking about the future—his editor mentioning an upcoming assignment, his wife discussing retirement plans—now feels unbearable. Samuel has come to believe that planning ahead is a kind of arrogance, a tempting of fate, because Kwame had been planning for his own recovery just days before he died. Similarly, overhearing conversations about loss, whether in the newsroom or at a dinner party, makes Samuel’s chest tighten. But the most potent trigger is incomprehensible chatter. In the newsroom, when two reporters speak over each other in rapid bursts, or when he walks through a crowded market and hears overlapping languages he cannot quite catch, the taste of metal floods his mouth. That taste is the first sign that the memory is coming. The chatter does not just remind him of the hospital; it *causes* the memory to break through. He will be standing at his desk, the noise around him rising, and suddenly he is back in that sterile room, Kwame’s hand in his, the doctors’ words dissolving into sound.

This has reshaped his daily life. Samuel now avoids the newsroom’s open-plan floor, preferring to work from a quiet corner where he can control the noise. He has stopped accepting assignments that require interviews in crowded spaces. His editor has noticed, and Samuel has already been passed over for a major feature. He tells himself it is temporary, but he is also certain that if he cannot explain what happened, no one will understand why he has changed. What frightens him most is the growing silence between him and his wife. She wants to talk about their future, about travel, about grandchildren, but every time she brings it up, Samuel feels the taste rise, and he cannot answer. He came to therapy because he is afraid that if this continues, he will lose her too—and he cannot find the words to tell her why.
